title: Gravitation
tagline: Kepler's laws, Newton's law of gravitation, acceleration due to gravity and its variation, gravitational potential and energy, escape speed, orbital speed and geostationary satellites.

Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Physics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Gravity is the force that keeps planets in orbit, holds the atmosphere around the Earth, and gives objects weight. This chapter develops the modern picture that began with Kepler's laws of planetary motion and was explained by Newton's law of universal gravitation. We then study how the acceleration due to gravity changes with altitude, latitude and depth, the idea of gravitational potential and potential energy, and the speeds needed for a satellite to stay in orbit or to escape the Earth. The chapter ends with a simple picture of geostationary satellites.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Kepler's laws; Newton's law of gravitation; g and its variation; gravitational field, potential and potential energy; escape velocity; orbital velocity; geostationary satellites

learningOutcomes: State Kepler's laws of planetary motion.
Explain why g = GM/R^2 on or near the Earth's surface.
Describe how g changes with altitude, latitude and depth.
Distinguish gravitational potential from gravitational potential energy.
Calculate escape speed and orbital speed for a satellite.
Explain the idea of a geostationary satellite.

blocks.text: Kepler stated three laws of planetary motion based on careful observation. The first law says that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. The second law says that the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. The third law says that the square of the period of a planet is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit. These laws describe how planets move, but they do not explain why.

items: Kepler's first law: elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.
Kepler's second law: equal areas in equal times.
Kepler's third law: T^2 is proportional to a^3.
The laws describe motion; they do not explain its cause.

items.text: A planet moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther away, in agreement with Kepler's second law.
items.note: Kepler's laws are about the shapes and timing of orbits, not about the force responsible for them.

blocks.text: Newton's law of gravitation says that every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. On or near the Earth, the Earth's pull on a body is its weight, and near the surface the weight is mg. The same gravitational law also explains the motion of the Moon and the planets when the calculations are done correctly.

items: F = G m1 m2 / r^2.
The force is attractive and acts along the line joining the particles.
Near Earth, weight = mg.
The same law explains planetary motion when applied properly.

items.text: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the force becomes one-quarter of its previous value, because the force depends on 1/r^2.
items.note: The inverse-square dependence is why gravity weakens rapidly as distance increases.

learn.title: Acceleration due to gravity and its variation

blocks.text: On the Earth's surface, the weight of a body is the gravitational force on it, so mg = GMm/R^2, giving g = GM/R^2. This explains why all bodies fall with the same acceleration in the same place if air resistance is ignored. Above the surface, g decreases with height; inside the Earth, g generally decreases with depth under a simple uniform-Earth model. The value of g also varies with latitude because the Earth is not perfectly spherical and because of rotation.

items: g = GM/R^2 at the surface.
g decreases with altitude.
g generally decreases with depth under a simple model.
Latitude affects g as well.

items.text: If a body is raised to a height equal to the Earth's radius R, the distance from the Earth's centre is 2R, so g_h is about g/4, because g_h/g = (R/(R+h))^2 = (R/2R)^2 = 1/4.
items.note: A common mistake is to think gravity halves when height equals R; it does not, because the distance from the centre doubles.

blocks.text: Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to that point. For a point mass, V = -GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m at that point is U = mV = -GMm/r, with zero taken at infinity. Near the Earth's surface, these ideas reduce to the familiar mgh for small changes. The negative sign shows that the force is attractive and that energy is released when a body falls toward the Earth.

items: Gravitational potential V = -GM/r for a point mass.
Gravitational potential energy U = -GMm/r.
Zero of potential energy is taken at infinity.
Negative values indicate a bound system.
For small height changes near the surface, Delta U is about mgh.

items.text: When a satellite moves higher, its gravitational potential energy becomes less negative, meaning energy must be supplied to raise it.
items.note: The negative value is not a mistake; it reflects the choice of zero at infinity.

blocks.text: Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed for a body to move away from a planet and never return, if it is moving under gravity alone. It can be found by equating kinetic energy to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy. For Earth, the escape speed is about 11 km/s. Escape speed depends on the mass and radius of the planet, not on the mass of the body being launched.

items: Escape speed ve = sqrt(2GM/R).
It depends on the planet's mass and radius.
It does not depend on the mass of the projectile.
It is derived by energy considerations.

items.text: A small object and a large object launched from the same height with the same escape speed would both have enough energy to escape, if air resistance were ignored.
items.note: Escape speed is a property of the planet, not of the object being launched.

blocks.text: A satellite staying in a circular orbit has gravity providing its centripetal acceleration. From this, the orbital speed is v_o = sqrt(GM/r). A geostationary satellite is one that stays above the same point on the equator and has a period of 24 hours. It must orbit in the same direction as the Earth's rotation and in an equatorial plane. Polar satellites, by contrast, pass over different parts of the Earth and serve different purposes.

items: For a circular orbit, v_o = sqrt(GM/r).
A satellite is not beyond gravity; gravity keeps it in orbit.
Geostationary satellites orbit above the equator with a 24-hour period.
Geostationary means it appears fixed above one point.

items.text: A satellite orbiting closer to the Earth must move faster than one farther away, because the gravitational pull is stronger at smaller radii.
items.note: This is one reason low Earth orbits are faster than higher ones.

keyPoints: Kepler's laws describe planetary motion; Newton's law explains it.
F = G m1 m2 / r^2, and near Earth weight = mg.
g = GM/R^2 on the Earth's surface.
g decreases with height; for h = R, g_h is about g/4.
Gravitational potential V = -GM/r and potential energy U = -GMm/r.
Escape speed ve = sqrt(2GM/R) and does not depend on the projectile's mass.
Orbital speed v_o = sqrt(GM/r) for a circular orbit.
examFocus: When calculating g at a height, use the distance from the Earth's centre, R + h, not just h.
Remember that zero of gravitational potential energy is taken at infinity; negative values do not mean the energy does not exist.

vocabulary.meaning: Three laws describing planetary motion around the Sun.
The law stating that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of distance.
Work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to a point.
The minimum speed needed to escape a planet's gravitational pull.
The speed needed for a satellite to stay in a circular orbit.
A satellite whose orbital period equals the Earth's rotation period, so it appears fixed above one point.

questions.prompt: Kepler's second law says that a planet sweeps out:
questions.explanation: Kepler's second law is the law of equal areas in equal times.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing it with equal distances, which is not what the law says.

questions.prompt: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force becomes:
questions.explanation: Gravitational force follows 1/r^2, so doubling the distance makes it one-quarter.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the force halves when distance doubles.

questions.prompt: Why is escape speed independent of the mass of the body being launched?
questions.answer: Escape speed comes from equating kinetic energy 1/2 m v^2 with the magnitude of gravitational potential energy, and the mass m cancels. So ve depends only on the planet, not on the projectile.
questions.explanation: The cancellation of m is why escape speed does not depend on the object's mass.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking heavier bodies need more escape speed, confusing energy needed with escape speed.

questions.prompt: Why is the value of g smaller at a height equal to Earth's radius R?
questions.answer: Because the distance from the Earth's centre becomes R + R = 2R, and g is proportional to 1/r^2, so g becomes about g/4.
questions.explanation: The decrease comes from the inverse-square law; the height is measured from the surface, but the distance is measured from the centre.
questions.commonMistake: Using h instead of R + h, which would wrongly give a smaller decrease.

questions.prompt: A satellite orbits at a height equal to Earth's radius R above the surface. What is the orbital speed in terms of the surface orbital speed v0, where v0 = sqrt(GM/R)?
questions.answer: Orbital speed v_o = sqrt(GM/r). Here r = R + R = 2R, so v_o = sqrt(GM/(2R)) = v0/sqrt(2).
questions.explanation: The orbital speed depends on sqrt(1/r), so increasing the orbital radius by a factor of 2 reduces the speed by sqrt(2).
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the speed stays the same or increases when the orbit is higher.
